q: Which glass is best for skylights?
n: Laminated glass stays in place when broken because the PVB interlayer holds the fragments. That is why codes favor it for skylights and overhead glazing. Source: ASTM C1172 (laminated glass); IBC Sec. 2405 (sloped glazing).

q: What glass is usually used for mall balustrades?
n: Laminated safety glass is used for mall balustrades because, if broken, it stays in the frame and still acts as a barrier against falls. Source: ASTM C1172; IBC Sec. 2407 (glass in guards).

q: What type of glass is commonly used for skylights?
n: Wired glass has long been used in skylights because the embedded wire holds broken glass in place so it does not fall on people below. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; NFPA 80.

q: What is the best glass for a shower stall?
n: Tempered glass is about four to five times stronger than annealed and breaks into small blunt cubes, so it is the standard safety glazing for shower stalls. Source: ASTM C1048; CPSC 16 CFR 1201 (safety glazing).

q: A client wants a glass partition between bedroom and T&B but needs privacy. Best option?
n: Etched (frosted) glass diffuses light and blocks the view, giving the toilet and bath privacy while still letting light through the partition. Source: Glass manufacturer literature; Ching, Interior Design Illustrated.

q: Why do convenience stores use glass storefronts?
n: Convenience stores use full glass storefronts so passers-by see the goods and activity inside. Visibility attracts customers and also aids surveillance. Source: Time-Saver Standards for Building Types (retail stores).

q: What material from oyster shells is used in window panels instead of glass?
n: Capiz is the translucent shell of the windowpane oyster (Placuna placenta), traditionally set in wooden lattice sliding windows (ventanillas) of the bahay na bato. Source: NCCA references on the bahay na bato; Perez, Encarnacion and Dacanay, Folk Architecture.

q: What is another name for etched glass?
n: Etched glass is classed with pattern (obscure) glass because its surface is worked to obscure the view while transmitting light. Source: Glass manufacturer literature; ASTM C1036 (patterned flat glass).

q: What differs between ordinary float glass and extra-clear glass?
n: Extra-clear (low-iron) glass is made with much less iron oxide than ordinary float glass, which removes the green tint and raises light transmission. Source: ASTM C1036; Pilkington Optiwhite product literature.

q: What type of glass should be used in museum display areas for rare artifacts?
n: Distortion-free float glass, usually laminated or low-iron, is used for museum display cases so rare artifacts are seen clearly without optical distortion. Source: ASTM C1036; museum display case manufacturer literature.

q: Mirrors with a distortion-free surface are made from:
n: Mirrors are made by silvering high-quality float glass because its flat, parallel surfaces give a distortion-free reflection. Source: ASTM C1503 (silvered flat glass mirror).

q: Which mirror do grocery stores use for security?
n: A convex mirror bulges outward, giving a wide-angle view of aisles and corners, so staff can watch for shoplifting. Source: Physics of mirrors; retail security guidance.

q: What glass is traditionally used in fire-exit doors?
n: Wired glass was traditionally used in fire-exit doors because the embedded mesh holds the glass together when heat cracks it, keeping the opening closed. Source: NFPA 80, Standard for Fire Doors; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which glass is used where distortion doesn't matter?
n: Drawn sheet glass is cheap but slightly wavy, so it is used only where some distortion does not matter, such as utility windows. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (glass types).

q: What glass is used for a luxury showroom?
n: Luxury showrooms use laminated safety glass because the interlayer resists smash-and-grab entry and holds together when hit, protecting goods and people. Source: ASTM C1172; glass manufacturer security glazing literature.

q: What type of glass is typically used for display windows?
n: Display windows use tempered glass for safety: it is stronger against impact and breaks into small blunt pieces if broken. Source: ASTM C1048; CPSC 16 CFR 1201 (safety glazing).

q: What glass is used for a second-floor glass floor with a clear view below?
n: A walk-on glass floor must be laminated (usually multi-ply tempered-laminated), so that if a ply breaks the others still carry the load and no one falls through. Source: ASTM E2751 (laminated glass in structural applications); glass manufacturer walk-on glass guidance.

q: What type of glass is dust-free?
n: When laminated glass breaks, its interlayer holds the fragments, so it does not shower the room with shards and fine glass dust the way other glass does. Source: ASTM C1172 (laminated architectural glass).

q: Which glass reduces both glare and solar heat entering the building?
n: Low-E glass has a microscopically thin metal-oxide coating that reflects infrared heat while transmitting visible light, cutting both solar heat gain and glare. Source: ASTM C1376 (coated glass); ASHRAE Handbook, Fundamentals (fenestration).

q: What happens when laminated glass is struck hard?
o: It breaks and splinters across the room
It breaks but the pieces stay bonded to the interlayer
n: Laminated glass has a PVB or ionoplast interlayer bonded between panes. When it is struck hard the glass cracks, but the fragments stay stuck to the interlayer and the pane stays in the frame. Source: ASTM C1172 (laminated architectural glass).

q: How is tempered glass cut on site?
o: It can't be cut on site
n: Tempered glass cannot be cut, drilled or edged after tempering: its built-in surface compression makes it shatter. All cutting and holes are done before the tempering furnace. Source: ASTM C1048 (heat-treated glass); glass fabricator guidance.

q: Which use best suits tempered glass?
n: Tempered glass suits shower doors, glass partitions and door glazing because it is strong and breaks into blunt cubes. It is not acoustic, bullet-resistant or burglar-resistant glazing. Source: ASTM C1048; CPSC 16 CFR 1201 (safety glazing).

q: Why is laminated glass recommended for skylights and overhead glazing?
o: It stays in place when broken
n: Laminated glass is recommended overhead because, when it breaks, the interlayer keeps the glass in place instead of letting it fall on people below. Source: IBC Sec. 2405 (sloped glazing and skylights); ASTM C1172.

q: For a high-end residential property next to a busy road, what is the best way to reduce noise?
n: Upgrading the windows (sealed double or laminated acoustic glazing) is the most effective noise fix, because windows are the weakest sound path in a facade facing traffic. Drapes absorb little low-frequency road noise. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics; ASTM E413 (STC ratings).

q: Which glass is used for acoustic insulation?
n: Double-glazed (insulating) units with an air space, especially with panes of different thickness or laminated glass, block much more sound than a single pane. Source: Egan, Architectural Acoustics; glass manufacturer acoustic data.

q: What glass is used for skylights and car windshields?
n: Skylights and car windshields both need glass that stays in place when broken. Laminated glass does this, because its interlayer holds the shards. Source: ASTM C1172; ANSI Z26.1 (automotive safety glazing).

q: Which glass has a mirror-like look?
n: Reflective glass has a metallic coating that gives a mirror-like look from the brighter side. Source: ASTM C1376 (pyrolytic and vacuum-deposition coatings on flat glass).

q: Which glass is NOT needed for interior use?
n: Low-E coatings control heat flow through the building envelope, so they are not needed for interior glazing. Interiors still use laminated, tempered or glass block where safety or privacy calls for it. Source: ASHRAE Handbook, Fundamentals (fenestration).

q: What is the standard thickness of a frameless glass shower door?
n: Frameless shower doors are typically 10 mm tempered glass, which is stiff enough to hang from hinges without a frame. 12 mm is used for large panels and 6–8 mm for framed doors. Source: Shower enclosure manufacturer literature; ASTM C1048.
